title: Overwhelmed by recalls? How to tell what's worth worrying about - USA Today

How to tell what's worth worrying about
 Mary Walrath-Holdridge USA TODAY Updated Oct. 28, 2026, 10:39 a.m. ET Hear this story Are you losing sleep over recalls ? 
 A seemingly never-ending barrage of product recalls, from lettuce and cheese to toothpaste and GLP-1 shots , can feel overwhelming and impossible to keep up with. For many Americans, especially after a string of high-profile outbreaks and product safety scares in recent years, recall headlines have become part of daily life. The result can be a nagging sense that nothing feels entirely safe anymore.
 The good news is that encountering a recall headline doesn't automatically mean you or your family are at risk.
 More: Trader Joe's wraps named as source of ongoing E. coli outbreak That's because recalls are not one-size-fits-all events. A recall notice may target retailers and not consumers. It may affect only people who purchased a product during a narrow time period. In many cases, the recall process works exactly as intended: identifying a potential problem, tracing affected products and removing them from the market before more people are harmed.
 USA TODAY Shopping: Shop sales in tech, home, fashion, beauty & more curated by our editors. A typo on packaging is certainly not the same as a listeria contamination linked to multiple deaths. Although both are recalls, they don't necessarily warrant the same level of attention – understanding that context can make recalls far less intimidating.
 When you feel that moment of panic, stop and reach for our recall guide instead.
 What is a recall?
 A product recall is the formal process by which a manufacturer or seller retrieves defective, unsafe or otherwise problematic products from the market to protect consumers. The goal is to remove the product from circulation and provide a remedy, such as a replacement, refund or repair. When a recall is injury- or illness-related, agencies like the Food and Drug Administration, the Department of Agriculture and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention pay extra attention.
 There are two main recalls: voluntary and mandatory. A voluntary recall is initiated by the manufacturer, distributor, seller or company responsible for the product, usually in tandem with the appropriate government agency. Meanwhile, government authorities, such as the FDA, initiate mandatory recalls when a company refuses or fails to act on a known safety issue.
 The example probably at the forefront of everyone's minds in 2026 is the summer's cyclospora outbreak, which sickened at least 20,000 people and killed two. The outbreak was traced to iceberg lettuce grown by the produce giant Taylor Farms, prompting recalls of some products. Multiple recall notices were issued because the lettuce was distributed nationwide to wholesalers, distributors, eateries and grocery stores, which repurposed it.
 Walmart had to recall its Taylor Farms-produced Marketside-branded lettuce, while Taco Bell made headlines over using the grower's potentially affected lettuce in some menu items. Because it was linked to a major outbreak, multiple government agencies got involved, and the recalls became part of a bigger investigation.
 Where to find recalls
 Agencies like the FDA and USDA issue notices for recalls they believe the public should know about. Recall notices are on the agencies' websites, where you can also sign up for email notifications. Sometimes, authorities or the recalling company will also contact consumers directly via email, phone or postal mail.
 The FDA regulates most food and drug products, except certain food items like meats, which the USDA oversees. If the FDA decides an issue affecting a product is large or urgent enough, it will issue a recall, market withdrawal or safety alert with information including the product name and type, reason for recall, identifying information and instructions for disposal or return. FDA actions can also be tracked through enforcement reports, which include recall classifications and recalls that weren't publicly notified. Recalls, Market Withdrawals, & Safety Alerts | FDA 
 Enforcement Reports | FDA 
 The USDA 's Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) handles recalls and public health alerts for items under its purview, like certain meat items and imported foods. Similar to FDA notices, they include identifying information about the recalled products. Recalls & Public Health Alerts | Food Safety and Inspection Service 
 The Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) covers recalls and product safety warnings about non-food and non-drug items. This can include anything from car seats and toys to generators and vacuums. These recall notices include product descriptions and information on when and where they were made and sold, which often includes online retailers like Amazon. Recalls & Product Safety Warnings | CPSC.gov 
 The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) deals with vehicle recalls and safety alerts. These include recalls for cars, tires, car seats and equipment. Check for Recalls: Vehicle, Car Seat, Tire, Equipment | NHTSA 
 USA TODAY maintains its own recall page that receives feeds from all of the above locations as they update. You can search our up-to-date database by category, including consumer products, food & drug, meat & poultry and automotive. Recalls | USA TODAY 
 The anatomy of a recall
 Recall notices vary by agency, but they generally follow similar formats. Check out our guide to navigating an FDA recall and spotting the information that is most important to you.
 Once you know what to look for, you can read all recalls with more confidence, FDA or otherwise.
 What to keep in mind and how to know if a recall affects you
 Not all recalls are created equal. Before going "recall crazy," learn what to look for.
 The entire grocery aisle isn't guilty by association
 When an item like lettuce is recalled, it's tempting to avoid the entire leafy greens section in the produce aisle. It's good to know which foods are higher risk and why (fresh produce and leafy greens commonly carry E. coli and salmonella), but specific item recalls are just that – specific. This is why you'll see details like lot codes and other identifiers in recall notices.
 Even the same product from the same store and grower/manufacter or seller can be safe if it was part of a different lot or shipment.
 Picture this: 
 You may spot two different store-brand veggie trays while shopping at your local grocery. They contain the same vegetables, dips and brand name, but one has enough food for 10-12 people, while another is intended to feed only 2-4.
 Then, there is a red bell pepper recall. Despite the trays being the same brand containing the same types of food sold at the same store, one could be recalled and one could not, even when they both have red bell peppers.
 This could be for a variety of reasons that demonstrate just how complex the U.S. food chain is: The manufacturer sourced the bell peppers from different places for each sized tray; the trays are processed and packaged at different facilities; different manufacturers make the tray packaging; one tray has peppers that are cut smaller and therefore were exposed to contaminated machinery that the others weren't; the peppers were grown and sold by the same business but at different locations; the peppers were grown by the same people at the same location but in different sections of soil or at slightly different times. The list goes on.
 "It’s understandable that consumers are cautious — recent GS1 US research found that over half of all consumers have avoided an entire food category after a recall," Angela Fernandez, a food safety expert at nonprofit GS1 US, which helps manage food safety infrastructure, previously told USA TODAY. 
 "But recalls are often more targeted than some people realize. Companies capture details about a product’s origin, movement and handling that can help investigators narrow down what was actually affected," she added. "That means a recall may apply only to a specific harvest or lot of certain products, purchase dates or regions, rather than all lettuce being sold nationwide."
 Not every recall concerns everyone
 A constant stream of headlines, push notifications and social media posts can feel overwhelming, as it can be impossible to tell what you actually need to worry about. But not every recall concerns everyone, and you can often find clues from the notice headline alone.
 Don't have kids? A major recall on baby formula or supplements probably isn't of much concern to you. Don't even know what alfalfa sprouts are? You probably don't need to panic when you see that alfalfa seed warning.
 If you're wondering if a recall may be relevant to you, ask yourself:
 What kind of product is this a recall for? A food, medication, car, consumer product? Do you usually purchase or own that type of product?
 Who is the recall for? Everyone? Consumers, retailers, distributors?
 Was the item only sold in certain states, during certain times, at certain retailers?
 Is the recall ongoing? Are items still on shelves? Is there an associated outbreak of illness or injury? If so, are people still getting sick?
 Download USA TODAY's app to get to the heart of news Lidl recalls gelato product sold in its US stores. See affected item Over 1.5M pounds of meat recalled includes hot dogs, bacon, more Raw cheddar cheese recalled over potential E. coli risk Smoked fish recalled in 6 states over listeria risk Workout drink recalled for illegal amphetamine-like substance The reason (and classification) matters
 Sometimes a product can be recalled for minor issues, such as a paperwork or packaging error. Other times, recalls can be triggered by serious health and safety concerns, such as medication or food being contaminated with deadly bacteria.
 For food, drugs and other products we consume, recall classifications often give you a hint. The FDA and USDA use a similar three-tiered system, with most USDA notices including an already-assigned classification, and many FDA recalls being assigned an official category by the agency, which it often adds later and makes viewable in its enforcement reports.
 The recall class and details in recall notices tell us the level of risk associated with using the product and how urgent it is. Before panicking because you have an affected product, check what its assigned class means.
 Class I: The most serious type of recall and the highest class level. This indicates a reasonable probability that the use of, or exposure to, a product may cause serious adverse health consequences or death. 
 For drugs, a Class I recall is urgent and generally involves removing the drug from the market and stopping all use. These recalls are generally conducted at the consumer level, meaning consumers possess the products directly and need to be told not to use them. Example: A medication or food tainted with potentially deadly bacteria.
 Class II: The classification for situations where the use of, or exposure to, a product may cause temporary or medically reversible adverse health consequences, or where the probability of serious adverse health consequences is remote.  For drugs, these recalls are generally conducted at the retail level, meaning they are pulled from shelves, but weren't directly given to consumers or aren't likely to be in consumers' hands. Patients and consumers can continue using the medicine unless the recalling company or FDA tells them otherwise. Example: A medication used for non-life-threatening issues, like Tylenol for headaches, is under strength and may not help the headache when taken as instructed.
 Class III: The least serious classification that means the use of, or exposure to, a product is not likely to cause adverse health consequences. For drugs, these recalls are generally conducted at the wholesale level, and patients and consumers can continue using the medicine unless the recalling company or FDA directs otherwise. Example: A food item has a minor labeling error.
 Market withdrawal: This occurs when a product has a minor violation that would not be subject to FDA legal action, and the firm removes the product from the market or corrects the violation. 
 Medical device safety alert: An alert issued in situations where a medical device may present an unreasonable risk of substantial harm. May also accompany a recall.
 As noted above, class II and class III drug recalls mean consumers can generally continue taking the medicine unless the recalling company provides other instructions.
 "In some instances, stopping your medicine may be more harmful to your health than continuing to take the recalled medicine," according to the FDA. "Talk to your doctor or pharmacist if you have questions or concerns about your medicine."
 Generally, class I drug recall notifications provide instructions with actions for patients.
 If a classification has not yet been provided, the safety or recall notice will instruct you on whether the product is safe to use or not. Typically, information like reported illnesses/injuries or possible effects of using the product will be included, which can also help indicate how serious and widespread an issue is.
 Determine your own tolerance for risk
 Ultimately, whether a product is "safe" to eat or use depends on your personal risk tolerance.
 Foodborne outbreaks have been traced to nearly every aisle of the grocery store, and no one precaution can guarantee a 100% success rate in avoiding illness. Toys have been infamously withdrawn for harming children and even some of the largest pharmaceutical companies have put out bad drug batches.
 Instead, people should weigh what is best for them and their families based on myriad factors like health history, vulnerability to or increased risk of serious illness or injury, access to healthcare, possible effects of the product and how vital use of the product is to you (do you need to take your insulin ASAP, for example).
 If you are a young, healthy adult who is okay with the possibility of a weekend on the toilet, you may choose to eat that burger despite recalled beef. If you're an immunocompromised cancer patient already struggling to fight off illness and keep food down, you'll probably be more likely to avoid burgers during that recall.
 "There is always a level of uncertainty when consuming food," Janet Buffer, senior institute manager for the Institute for Food Safety and Nutrition Security with The George Washington University's Milken Institute School of Public Health, previously told US TODAY . "And every individual must determine their level of risk tolerance."
